The keys to remember

Alt+Jgo where Pair points
Alt+Ytake Pair’s suggested change
Alt+↑in the chat: pick a message, then act on it
/gen here …ask for code; /undo takes it back

github.com/makefunstuff/pairing-buddy
Pairing buddy, or Pair for short,
is a pair programmer that sits beside you in Neovim.
It watches while you work, and speaks only when something matters.
Its words appear where you are already looking.
And it changes your code only when you hand it the wheel.
This tutorial shows each of these, one at a time.
First, the screen you will see in every scene.
Watch the four labelled areas.
On the left is Neovim, with your code.
Under it is your terminal, where you run commands.
On the right is Pair’s chat.
It keeps a record of what Pair says, and you can type to it.
And along the bottom, the statusline shows what Pair is doing right now.
Your code, your terminal, the chat, and the statusline.
Pair uses all four.
Pair is a Neovim plugin and a small
program that runs in the background, the daemon.
Watch the last lines of each command.
One npm command installs it, straight from GitHub.
Then pair setup writes a config file from the example, offers a login,
and starts the daemon as a service, so it runs from now on.
Last, it says what to add to Neovim:
the plugin, for lazy dot nvim, or any plugin manager.
Two commands:
Pair is installed, and its daemon runs as a service.
Pair needs a model:
a server on your machine, or a cloud provider with a key.
Watch the ticks pair doctor prints.
The config names one model for both jobs.
This tutorial uses DeepSeek, in the cloud.
Pair auth stores the key, in a file only you can read.
It never prints it.
Then pair doctor checks every part:
the service, the daemon, the plugin in Neovim,
the sandbox for commands, and the model itself.
It asks the model a question, times the answer, and checks that it thinks.
A cross, instead of a tick, would name the fix.
A config, a key, and pair doctor:
every part checked before you start.
Two models share the work.
The Watcher is small and fast.
It scores every moment from zero to ten:
is this worth a word?
Only high scores reach the Partner.
It thinks first, reads your code, and writes what Pair says.
One model can play both parts.
The Partner works in one of three roles, and the statusline always says which.
Navigator is the default.
It watches, and points at code.
Scout runs commands for you, in a pane of its own, inside a sandbox.
And Driver types one change into your buffer, then gives the wheel back.
You want to know why a test fails, without digging yourself.
Watch the chat, and the pane at the bottom.
In the chat, slash scout switches Pair to the Scout role.
The header says so.
Then you ask your question, in plain words.
Scout runs the test in Pair’s own pane at the bottom,
where you can see every command, in a sandbox:
only the project is writable, and there is no network.
The answer comes back in the chat, and under your line in Neovim:
the greater-or-equal on line thirty-five rejects the wait that fits exactly.
You asked once; Scout ran the test in plain sight and answered.

Under it, its action line:

Alt up picks the message,

Plus rates it useful.
Every remark lands in the chat too, with the keys that act on it.

A test fails, and you start fixing the wrong file.
Watch the margin, under the line you change.
In your terminal, the delivery test fails:
it wants five attempts, and gets four.
You guess the backoff is wrong, and change the shift on line twenty.
Pair saw the red test,
and an edit in a file the failure doesn’t name.
The Watcher scores that a wrong turn, worth a word.
So the Partner reads the code, and speaks once, under the line you changed.
The cause is the greater-or-equal in worker dot go.
Alt J goes where it points.
Your cursor never moves by itself.
Pair spoke once, where you were looking, and pointed at the real cause.
You fix one line, and a test somewhere else breaks.
Watch the statusline, then the ghost text.
Each time you save, Pair runs your tests,
in its own pane at the bottom.
The delivery test is red.
You fix the check on line thirty-five, from greater-or-equal to greater, and save again.
Delivery passes now, but a queue test that passed before now fails.
That is a regression, and the Watcher scores it high.
Pair says why, under your line:
the queue’s lease is only the budget,
and attempt five starts just as it ends.
Alt J goes to its fix, in queue dot go.
The ghost text shows the old line struck through,
and the new lines under it.
Nothing has changed yet.
Alt Y takes it into your buffer.
You save, the tests run again, and they pass.
Pair ran the tests you might skip, caught a regression,
and showed its fix before you took it.
You are writing a design note, not code yet.
Watch the margin of the note.

When you stop, Pair reads the whole note, and the code it names.
Its notes land in the margin, each with a sign.
A question mark is a question the note leaves open.
The not-equal sign marks two lines that can’t both be true:
five attempts here, six there.
The arrow says what the code really does.
Here, the note is wrong about worker dot go.
Nothing in the note changed.
The marks are only in the margin.

You want edge cases added to a table test, and you’d rather watch.

You hand over with Pair drive, and say what you want.
Pair is the Driver now.
The statusline says it has the wheel.
It reads the test and the code first.
Then it types, into your buffer, where you can see every line arrive.
It runs the tests on the unsaved buffer, in its own pane at the bottom,
and hands the wheel back with a short note.
Nothing is saved yet.
U takes the whole change away in one step,
and control R brings it back.
Pair typed one change in plain sight, tested it, and gave the wheel back.
Pair is typing, and you change your mind.
Watch the lines it types, and the chat.
The same hand-over as before.
Pair starts typing the cases.
You press any key.
The typing stops, and what it typed is gone, as if it never started.
The chat says you have the wheel back, and Pair is the Navigator again.
Any key takes the wheel back, and nothing Pair typed stays behind.
Pair writes code when you ask for it, and only then.
You ask with slash gen, in one of five shapes.
Here is code at your cursor.
File makes new files, as buffers to review.
Try writes a sample to run, outside your project.
Scaffold builds many files and their wiring, away from your project.
And board hands the work to another agent.
Whatever the shape, nothing reaches your project until you take it.
You want a small method, right under your cursor.
Watch the gen card in the chat, then your code.
In the chat, slash gen here, and what you want.
Your cursor in Neovim says where it goes.
The request gets a number, and runs on its own.
Its card shows the code as a diff, with its keys,
and Neovim shows it as ghost lines under your cursor.
Alt up picks the card, and K keeps it:
the code lands in your buffer, unsaved, as one undo step,
and the tests run on it.
The thin bar in the sign column marks code that is not yours yet.
It stays until you edit it, or say Pair own.
Slash undo takes the whole request back, in one step.
Asked for, kept with one key,
marked until you own it, undone in one step.
Your notes say logs go through slog,
and you ask for f m t dot printf.
Watch the question in the chat.
Every request runs against the brief:
the session’s goal and your notes, NOTES dot md by default.
Pair reads it, and never edits it.
This request goes against a line of it,
so Pair asks first, and quotes the line.
Y goes as asked, N follows the brief, and E opens the note there.
You press N.
The code follows the brief:
slog, not printf.
And the card says where it went against your words.
Your notes are the brief:
Pair asks before it goes against them.
You want a new test file.
Watch the gen card, then Neovim.
Slash gen file asks for new files.
It comes back as a buffer to review, and nothing is on disk yet.
Its check ran your tests with it:
here, the new test fails, and the card says why.
Schedule overflows past thirty attempts.
K opens the file in Neovim.
Its winbar says it is generated, and that colon w takes it.
Colon w writes it to its path:
your own save is the one way Pair’s code reaches your disk.
The tests run, and the bar marks lines that are not yours yet.
New files arrive as buffers to review; your :w takes them.
You want to see an idea run before it touches your project.
Watch the split, then the chat.
Slash gen try writes a sample in a folder of its own,
outside the project.
Pair runs it in its pane, in a sandbox:
only that folder is writable, and there is no network.
The sample opens in a split, as a real file.
Change it, and the run key runs it again.
The card says how its run went.
Slash keep moves it into the project, as a buffer to review.
Try it outside the project; /keep moves in what you want.
You want a small command and its test, wired to your code.
Watch the gen card.
Slash gen scaffold builds many files and their wiring away from your project.
With dash dash branch, in a git worktree, on a branch of its own.
Pair wrote it, built it and ran the tests there.
The card lists every file, new or changed,
how the check went, and what it guessed.
K puts slash keep on the line, with the scaffold’s files in a menu.
Enter keeps one, as a buffer to review.
No key keeps them all:
you read each one.
A scaffold is built aside; you keep it a file at a time.
Some work is too big to watch:
it should be another agent’s task.
Watch the chat.
Slash gen board hands it to the board, Shepherdr, as a task.
No model runs.
Pair writes the task’s brief from yours,
and shows the whole command before anything is added.
Each pick is one key.
Y adds it for later, and D adds it and delegates it.
P asks for a plan first, R for research only,
and C copies the command.
You press D.
The board adds the task, and its agent starts on the brief.
One request, one key:
a task for another agent.
While you work, another agent finishes its task.
Watch the statusline and the chat, when you save.
You type, and Pair holds the news:
it never speaks while you type.
You save, a breakpoint, and one line says it:
in the statusline, and in the chat, with its keys.
Pair agents lists every task, the ones that need you first.
O opens its report or pull request, and D its branch’s diff, read only.
And T opens a terminal in its worktree.
Other agents’ news waits for your pause, with keys to what they left.
A task is ready to merge.
Read it before it lands.
Watch the review list.
Alt R, on the line of a task ready to merge,
opens its branch as a review.
Pair review, and the task, does the same.
On top, what its reviewer said, and what is not proven.
Then what the branch guessed that your brief does not settle.
Then its files.
K keeps one in your checkout, unsaved and marked,
for you to make your own.
Review a task’s branch, and keep the pieces you want.
Another agent is changing the file you have open.
Watch the top of the window, then under your line.
Each task’s agent works in its own worktree,
and Pair reads what its branch changes.
The winbar says this file is one of them.
You change the same line, and save.
Pair says what the other task writes there,
and that whichever merges second meets a conflict.
The chat has it too.
Pair tells you before two agents’ changes collide.
Your notes moved on since your task’s brief was written.
Watch the chat.
You work on a board task’s branch.
Slash brief sync says what the task’s brief
on the board lacks from NOTES dot md.
Y tells the task’s agent, C copies the command, and N leaves it.
/brief sync keeps the board’s task in step with your notes.
You can work in several git worktrees at once.
A project is the git root of the folder Neovim starts in.
So each worktree is a project of its own,
with its own session, goal, chat and memory.
To switch, go to the Neovim you started in the other worktree,
rather than colon c d in this one.
A scaffold made with dash dash branch is a worktree too.
Open a Neovim there, and it pairs on its own.
Your hands are on the code, and a question comes up.
Watch the line under your cursor.
Hold Alt T, and ask out loud.
The meter shows Pair hears you.
Let go, and whisper dot c p p writes down what it heard,
on your own machine.
That is your question, under your line.
Then Pair answers in the same place, and marks line thirty-five.
Alt J would go there.
You asked out loud, and the answer came where you were looking.
Voice is off until you set it up.
No whisper dot c p p to build?
OpenRouter can hear you instead,
and read the answer aloud when you are away from the editor.
Name its models and your key in the config, and pair doctor checks them.
The recording then leaves your machine.
Pair works with or without herdr, the terminal workspace for coding agents.
Without it, one Neovim holds everything.
Pair chat opens the chat,
and Pair’s own pane is a terminal at the bottom.
Every scene you just saw ran this way.
With herdr, the chat and Pair’s pane are panes of their own.
Pair also sees the agents herdr runs, and terminals outside Neovim.
Either way, it is the same Pair, with the same keys.
Here are the keys to remember.
Alt J goes where Pair points, and Alt Y takes its suggested change.
In the chat, Alt up picks a message, to act on it.
Slash gen here asks for code, and slash undo takes it back.
Pair drive hands over one change, and any key takes the wheel back.
Pair agents shows your other agents, and Alt R reviews a task.
Hold Alt T to ask out loud,
and run pair doctor whenever something seems off.
Pairing buddy is on GitHub.
Happy pairing.
